where: Погода: ветер идёт вдоль изобар, а не поперёк; циклон в северном полушарии закручен против часовой стрелки, в южном — по
Пассаты: воздух, стекающий от тридцатых широт к экватору, приходит туда с северо-востока, а не с севера
Артиллерия: снос 61 м на 20 км входит в таблицы стрельбы наравне с поправками на ветер и температуру заряда
Маятник Фуко: полный оборот плоскости качания за 23,93 ч / sin φ — 31,8 ч в Париже, 48,8 ч в Эль-Кувейте
Океан: дрейфующие буи наматывают инерционные петли радиусом порядка километра с периодом 11,97 ч / sin φ
memo.watchOut: Три ловушки. Первая — путать расстояние до ОСИ с расстоянием до центра: в центробежном члене стоит $r_{\perp}$, и на полюсе он равен нулю, хотя радиус Земли там никуда не делся. Вторая — прибавлять центробежную силу к весу: стандартное $g$ её уже содержит, потому что весы вращаются вместе с планетой, и второе прибавление — двойной счёт. Третья — объяснять центробежной силой приливы и воронку в раковине: в первом случае это верный ответ по неверной причине, во втором — эффект в тысячи раз слабее того, что реально задаёт направление.

quiz.q: Снаряд выпущен строго на юг из точки на широте 50° северной широты. В какую сторону его снесёт кориолисовой силой?
options: На запад: в северном полушарии снос всегда вправо от направления движения, а справа от юга — запад
На восток: Земля вращается на восток и увлекает снаряд за собой
Никуда: при движении вдоль меридиана снос обращается в ноль
На юг, то есть снаряд просто перелетит: сила направлена вдоль скорости
quiz.why: Горизонтальная кориолисова сила равна $m f v$ и стоит перпендикулярно скорости, отклоняя вправо в северном полушарии — при любом направлении стрельбы. Смотрим на юг, поворачиваем вправо — получаем запад. Ответ «на восток» путает две разные вещи: увлечение вращением уже сидит в переносной скорости и в неподвижной системе даёт прямолинейный полёт, а снос — это как раз то, что остаётся сверх него. Ответ «никуда» проверяется прямо по формуле: обращается в ноль не меридиональное движение, а движение вдоль оси вращения, и на широте 50° горизонтальная скорость с осью не совпадает. Ответ «сила направлена вдоль скорости» противоречит основному свойству: $\vec F_{\text{кор}}\perp\vec v$, и потому вдоль скорости эта сила не даёт ничего вообще.
quiz.hint: Сила перпендикулярна скорости и в северном полушарии отклоняет вправо. Встаньте лицом на юг и покажите рукой вправо — куда вы показали?

quiz.q: Кориолисова сила перпендикулярна скорости при любом движении. Какое следствие из этого верно?
options: Она не совершает работы: кинетическую энергию тела во вращающейся системе она изменить не может
Она не влияет на траекторию, а только на показания приборов
Она равна нулю для тела, покоящегося во вращающейся системе, и потому не участвует ни в каких задачах
Она всегда меньше центробежной, потому что перпендикулярные силы слабее продольных
quiz.why: Мощность силы есть скалярное произведение $\vec F\cdot\vec v$, а у перпендикулярных векторов оно равно нулю. Значит кориолисова сила меняет только направление скорости и не может ни разогнать тело, ни затормозить его. Ответ про одни лишь показания приборов неверен грубо: траектория как раз и гнётся, дуга на вращающемся листе — прямое тому доказательство. Ответ про покоящееся тело верен наполовину и потому опасен: да, для покоящегося тела сила равна нулю (в формуле стоит $\vec v_{\text{отн}}$), но именно движущиеся тела и составляют весь предмет — ветер, снаряд, буй. Ответ «перпендикулярные силы слабее продольных» — просто вымысел: отношение кориолисова члена к центробежному ускорению самого потока, $v^{2}/L$, и есть число Россби, и у циклона кориолисов член на порядок больше.
quiz.hint: Мощность силы равна $\vec F\cdot\vec v$. Чему равно скалярное произведение двух перпендикулярных векторов?

quiz.q: Своими словами: откуда в формуле F = 2m[v×ω] взялась именно двойка? Назовите два механизма, каждый из которых даёт по ω·v·dt.
quiz.why: Первый механизм: вектор относительной скорости разворачивается вместе с полом. За время $dt$ вся система повернулась на угол $\omega\,dt$, стрелка скорости повернулась вместе с ней, и приращение поперёк движения равно $\omega v\,dt$. Второй механизм: тело сместилось по радиусу, а скорость самого пола растёт с радиусом как $\omega r_{\perp}$. Уехав наружу на $v\,dt$, тело должно догнать пол, разогнавшись по окружности ещё на $\omega v\,dt$, — иначе оно от него отстанет. Два разных счёта дают одинаковый ответ, поэтому множитель ровно 2. Ту же двойку можно получить и третьим путём, из производной произведения $r\dot\theta$ в полярных координатах, — и совпадение трёх независимых выводов и есть лучшая проверка результата.
quiz.hint: Одно связано с тем, что поворачивается сам вектор скорости. Второе — с тем, что скорость пола зависит от расстояния до оси, а тело это расстояние меняет.

quiz.q: Маятник Фуко подвешен на широте 60°. За сколько часов плоскость его качания сделает полный оборот? Звёздные сутки считайте равными 23,93 часа. Ответ в часах.
quiz.why: Плоскость качания поворачивается со скоростью $\Omega\sin\varphi$, поэтому период равен $T = 23{,}93/\sin\varphi$. Синус шестидесяти градусов равен $\sqrt{3}/2 = 0{,}866$, значит $T = 23{,}93/0{,}866 = 27{,}6$ часа, то есть примерно 13 градусов в час. Проверка на предельных случаях: на полюсе синус равен единице и период равен звёздным суткам ровно — маятник качается в неподвижной плоскости, а Земля проворачивается под ним; на экваторе синус равен нулю, период бесконечен, поворота нет вовсе. Шестьдесят градусов — это широта Санкт-Петербурга, и маятник в Исаакиевском соборе, работавший с 1931 по 1986 год, действительно поворачивался примерно на 13 градусов в час.
quiz.hint: Период равен звёздным суткам, делённым на синус широты. Синус шестидесяти градусов — это 0,87, значит ответ должен быть чуть больше суток.

en.title: Rotating system: centrifugal force and Coriolis
en.subtitle: Section 3 · Where forces with no source come from
intro: Place a plate on the table, put a sheet of paper on it, and spin it. Now take a ruler, press it against the table—not against the plate, against the table—and draw a straight line with a marker along the ruler across the rotating sheet. Remove the sheet: there is an arc on it. The ruler was straight, the hand moved straight, the table did not move, but the trace is curved. No one pushed the sheet sideways, and yet it recorded a turn.

This is the whole section in one experiment. An observer attached to the rotating sheet sees motion along an arc and must name the cause: since the trajectory bends, there must be a force. He will not be able to find its source—there is no rope, no magnet, no neighboring body that exerts this force. What inertial force is and why it is no worse than ordinary force, we have already discussed in the topic 'Oscillations and rotation'; here we will not repeat that, but will immediately calculate—we will get all the terms that ever appear in a rotating system, and not a single extra one.

The body in this section is a point. Neither moment of inertia nor angular momentum, which we dealt with in the first two sections of the topic, will be needed: we will talk not about the rotation of the body, but about the rotation of the view on the body. Along the way, we will have to introduce one thing that has not appeared anywhere in the course so far—the tangential-normal decomposition of acceleration. Let's start with that.
en.standNote: The topic stand has three modes; you need the third one, 'Drift'. The platform with a radius of 0.5 m rotates, a ball is released from the center, and the stand draws its flight with two traces at once: a straight line in the fixed system and an arc in the system attached to the platform. Both traces describe the same motion, the difference is only in who is watching. Set the angular velocity to 2.0 rad/s and the ball speed to 2.0 m/s—these are the values we will analyze in the text. The stand will label the Coriolis acceleration $a = 2\omega v = 8$ m/s², and the ball, flying the entire radius in a quarter of a second, will drift sideways by 0.25 m—half the radius of the platform. Pay attention to two things. First: the straight trace remains straight no matter what you do with the $\omega$ slider—in the fixed system there is no force and never was. Second: set $\omega = 0$, and the arc straightens out, and the Rossby number on the display flies off to infinity. This is the same kitchen experiment from 'Entertaining Physics', only instead of a platform there is a plate, and instead of a ball there is a marker.

formula.name: Acceleration in a rotating system: centrifugal term and Coriolis force
formula.latex: \vec a_{\text{fixed}} = \vec a_{\text{rel}} + 2\,\vec\omega\times\vec v_{\text{rel}} + \vec\omega\times(\vec\omega\times\vec r) \qquad \vec F_{\text{cor}} = 2m\,[\vec v_{\text{rel}}\times\vec\omega]
formula.alsoKnown: Coriolis theorem on the composition of accelerations; compound centrifugal acceleration (as Coriolis himself called it). In meteorology, the same term is written using the Coriolis parameter f = 2Ω·sin φ

authors.what: in his work 'On centrifugal force' was the first to calculate the force with which a spinning body pulls on a rope, and obtained the dependence on the square of the velocity and inversely on the radius — this is the future third term of our formula
in the tidal equations already wrote out a term proportional to the flow velocity and the sine of the latitude, but did not single it out as a separate general phenomenon

in the article 'On the equations of relative motion of systems of bodies' obtained the missing term in general form and called it compound centrifugal acceleration; he was thinking not about the planet, but about machines — water wheels and gear trains, where parts move inside rotating components
hung a pendulum and showed the rotation of the plane of oscillation — the first direct, room-sized proof of the Earth's rotation, requiring no astronomical observations
transferred all this to the atmosphere and explained why the wind blows not across the isobars, but along them, and why cyclones in the two hemispheres rotate in opposite directions

formula.story: The name on the formula is an engineer's. Coriolis taught mechanics at the École Polytechnique and worked on machine theory — his real fame lies elsewhere: it was he who introduced the word 'work' into physics in its current sense, as force multiplied by distance. The problem from which the extra term grew was workshop-level: how to calculate the motion of a part that moves along the spoke of a rotating wheel. There is no weather, no oceans, no Earth in the 1835 article at all. Meteorology was brought to this term by Ferrel twenty years later, and the expression 'Coriolis force' itself came into common use only around the 1920s, in the Scandinavian school of weather forecasting. It is also amusing that the first to get a practical answer were not physicists but sailors: the Dutchman Buys Ballot in 1857 formulated a rule that still works without any formulas — stand with your back to the wind in the northern hemisphere, and the low-pressure area will be on your left.

symbols.what: angular velocity of the rotating system
symbols.note: vector along the axis of rotation by the right-hand rule; in this section we consider it constant

symbols.what: velocity of the body measured in the rotating system
symbols.note: exactly what an observer on a carousel sees, not what an observer on the ground sees

symbols.what: acceleration of the body in the rotating system
symbols.note: it is to this that the sum of real forces plus two additions is equated — this is the whole point of the derivation

symbols.what: component of the radius vector perpendicular to the axis
symbols.note: distance to the AXIS, not to the center: at the pole it is zero, at the equator it is the Earth's radius

symbols.what: tangential and normal unit vectors of the trajectory
symbols.note: τ points forward along the motion, n points inward of the turn, perpendicular to τ

symbols.what: radius of curvature of the trajectory
symbols.note: radius of the circle that best fits the curve at a given point; for a straight line it is infinite

symbols.what: Coriolis parameter
symbols.note: f = 2Ω·sin φ — what 2ω becomes for horizontal motion over the Earth's surface; zero at the equator

symbols.what: Rossby number
symbols.note: Ro = v/(fL) — how many times the flow's own inertia is stronger than Coriolis; the entire measure of the effect's importance in one number

derivation.title: Rigorous Derivation
derivation.lead: We need exactly two things: the definition of the derivative of a vector and the definition of the cross product. No tensors, no rotation matrices—only the geometry of displacement over time $dt$. We assume the reader is already familiar with the concept of inertial force and why it has no source from the topic 'Oscillations and Rotation'; here we do not introduce it anew but derive it in general form.

steps.text: Let's start with geometry, without any rotation of frames. Velocity is always tangent to the trajectory, so we can write it as its magnitude times a unit tangent vector: $\vec v = v\,\vec\tau$. Differentiating this product yields exactly two terms. The first accounts for the body moving faster or slower. The second accounts for the rotation of the vector $\vec\tau$ itself. A unit vector cannot change its length, so its derivative is perpendicular to it and points toward the inside of the turn; its magnitude equals the rate of change of the path direction, i.e., $v/\rho$. In summary: any acceleration decomposes into 'faster-slower' along the motion and 'sharper-flatter' across it.
steps.figCaption: Acceleration always splits into two parts: along the motion it changes the speed, across it changes the direction

steps.text: Now the main lemma from which everything else will follow. Take a vector $\vec A$ that is fixed in the rotating frame—say, drawn with chalk on a carousel. For an observer on the ground, it still changes: over time $dt$ the whole carousel rotates by angle $\omega\,dt$, and the tip of the vector moves along a circle of radius $|\vec A|\sin\alpha$, where $\alpha$ is the angle between $\vec A$ and the axis. The displacement length equals the radius of that circle times the rotation angle, and the direction is perpendicular to both the axis and the vector itself. These three properties—magnitude $|\vec A|\,\omega\sin\alpha$, perpendicularity to both, and right-handed triple—are exactly the definition of the cross product $\vec\omega\times\vec A$. If the vector also changes in the rotating frame, the two causes add.
steps.figCaption: The tip of a vector fixed on a carousel traces a circle of radius |A|·sin α—this is where the cross product ω×A comes from

steps.text: Apply the lemma to the position vector of the body. On the left is the velocity seen by a stationary observer; on the right is the velocity seen by an observer on the carousel, plus a correction. The meaning of the correction is simple and worth stating: $\vec\omega\times\vec r$ is the velocity of that point of the carousel that the body is currently passing. It is called the transport velocity. The body, as it were, 'inherits' the motion of the floor beneath it: if it sat still on the carousel, its entire velocity for an earthly observer would be just this transport velocity.
steps.figCaption: Velocity for an earthly observer = velocity relative to the carousel + velocity of that point of the floor over which the body is currently located

steps.text: Now apply the lemma a SECOND time—not to the position vector, but to the velocity from the previous step. The lemma holds for any vector, not just $\vec r$; that is its main virtue. The substitution rule is conveniently remembered as an operator: to take the fixed derivative, take the rotating one and add $\vec\omega\times$. Apply it to the sum $\vec v_{\text{rel}} + \vec\omega\times\vec r$, assuming $\vec\omega$ is constant, and collect terms. There are three of them, and one is doubled—this deserves a closer look.
steps.latex: \vec a_{\text{fixed}} = \left(\frac{d}{dt}\right)_{\text{rot}}\!\!\bigl(\vec v_{\text{rel}} + \vec\omega\times\vec r\bigr) + \vec\omega\times\bigl(\vec v_{\text{rel}} + \vec\omega\times\vec r\bigr) = \vec a_{\text{rel}} + 2\,\vec\omega\times\vec v_{\text{rel}} + \vec\omega\times(\vec\omega\times\vec r)
steps.figCaption: The lemma is applied twice—to the position vector and to the velocity; of the four terms, two turn out to be identical and yield the factor of two

steps.text: Where the factor of two comes from is not an arithmetic question but a physical one, and the answer is beautiful: two completely different mechanisms contribute equally. First: the relative velocity vector simply rotates with the floor. Over time $dt$ the floor rotates by $\omega\,dt$, and with it the velocity arrow—an increment $\omega v\,dt$ perpendicular to the motion. Second: the body moves radially, and the transport velocity $\omega r_{\perp}$ depends on the radius. Moving outward by $v\,dt$, the body must speed up along the circle by another $\omega\,v\,dt$, otherwise it would lag behind the floor. Two different calculations, two identical answers—hence the factor is exactly 2, not 1 or 3. Check the limiting case: if the body moves parallel to the rotation axis, its velocity has nowhere to turn, and the radius does not change—so the Coriolis term vanishes, as the cross product shows.
steps.latex: \underbrace{\omega v\,dt}_{\text{velocity vector } \vec v_{\text{rel}} \text{ rotated}} + \underbrace{\omega v\,dt}_{\text{transport velocity } \omega r_{\perp} \text{ increased}} = 2\,\omega v\,dt \;\Longrightarrow\; \vec a_{\text{cor}} = 2\,\vec\omega\times\vec v_{\text{rel}}
steps.figCaption: Two mechanisms, the same contribution ω·v·dt: on the left the velocity vector rotates, on the right the speed of the floor itself under the body increases

steps.text: It remains to write Newton's second law as the observer on the carousel wants to see it. They can only measure $\vec a_{\text{rel}}$, so the extra terms must be moved to the right, changing sign. The double cross product is expanded by the identity $\vec\omega\times(\vec\omega\times\vec r) = \vec\omega(\vec\omega\cdot\vec r) - \omega^{2}\vec r = -\omega^{2}\vec r_{\perp}$, i.e., after moving it gives a term directed OUTWARD from the axis and growing as $\omega^{2}$—this is the centrifugal force. The second term, after moving, is conveniently written by swapping the order of factors: $-2m\,\vec\omega\times\vec v = 2m\,[\vec v\times\vec\omega]$. Look at it carefully. It is perpendicular to the velocity—always, for any motion. Hence its dot product with velocity is zero, so it does no work and can neither speed up nor slow down the body. It can do exactly one thing: turn.
steps.latex: m\,\vec a_{\text{rel}} = \vec F + \underbrace{m\,\omega^{2}\vec r_{\perp}}_{\text{centrifugal, outward}} + \underbrace{2m\,[\vec v_{\text{rel}}\times\vec\omega]}_{\text{Coriolis, }\perp\vec v} , \qquad \vec F_{\text{cor}}\cdot\vec v_{\text{rel}} = 0
steps.figCaption: Two additions of different nature: centrifugal depends on location and pulls from the axis, Coriolis depends on velocity and stands perpendicular to it

steps.text: Now move to Earth. The vector $\vec\Omega$ points along the Earth's axis, and we are interested in horizontal motion on the surface—a train, wind, a projectile. Decompose $\vec\Omega$ at latitude $\varphi$ into a vertical component $\Omega\sin\varphi$ and a horizontal component $\Omega\cos\varphi$ directed northward. Only the vertical part can turn velocity within the horizontal plane: the horizontal part gives a vertical force, which is entirely swallowed by weight. Hence the Coriolis parameter $f = 2\Omega\sin\varphi$: the horizontal acceleration equals $f v$ and is always directed to the right of motion in the Northern Hemisphere and to the left in the Southern, regardless of which direction you are traveling. At the equator, the sine is zero and there is no horizontal deflection at all. The Foucault pendulum—same factor: its plane of oscillation rotates at speed $\Omega\sin\varphi$, i.e., a full turn takes a sidereal day divided by the sine of latitude.
steps.figCaption: At latitude φ only the vertical part Ω·sin φ matters: it turns horizontal motions to the right in the Northern Hemisphere

steps.text: The last question is the most practical: when is Coriolis important, and when can we forget about it? Compare two accelerations: the intrinsic one associated with the curvature of the flow over its characteristic size $L$, i.e., of order $v^{2}/L$, and the Coriolis acceleration $f v$. Their ratio is the Rossby number $\mathrm{Ro} = v/(fL)$. Small Ro means Coriolis dominates: for a cyclone of a thousand kilometers with wind 10 m/s, we get 0.097, and therefore the wind goes not across isobars toward low pressure, but almost along them. Large Ro means it drowns in everything else: for a sink vortex 20 centimeters wide with speed 0.3 m/s, we get $1{,}5\cdot10^{4}$—four orders of magnitude. Between them lies artillery: for a projectile at 20 kilometers, Ro is about 160, the deflection is only 61 meters over the entire range—but the target is already missed, and the correction is entered into firing tables.
steps.figCaption: One dimensionless number puts everything in its place: the smaller Ro, the more Coriolis governs the motion

derivation.plate: m\,\vec a_{\text{rel}} = \vec F + m\,\omega^{2}\vec r_{\perp} + 2m\,[\vec v_{\text{rel}}\times\vec\omega]
derivation.plateCap: On the left is what the observer on the carousel measures with a ruler and a stopwatch. On the right is the real force, which has a source, and two additions that have no source. The first depends only on WHERE the body is, the second only on WHERE and how fast it moves. They cannot be removed, but they are not superfluous: they are the price for the right to consider the rotating floor stationary.
derivation.note: Three caveats, each of which later surfaces in problems. First: we assumed $\vec\omega$ is constant. If the carousel spins up or brakes, another term appears on the right-hand side, $-m\,\dfrac{d\vec\omega}{dt}\times\vec r$—it is called the Euler force, and it is discussed in detail in the appendix. For Earth it is negligible: the day lengthens by about two milliseconds per century. Second: our body is a point. A real extended body in a rotating frame also experiences a difference of these forces across its ends, and if it itself rotates, moment of inertia and gyroscopic effects come into play—all that is the first two paragraphs of the topic, and we do not bring it here. Third, and most insidious: the centrifugal term on Earth has already been accounted for. When you weigh something on kitchen scales, you measure not the gravitational force but its sum with the centrifugal force, because the scales rotate with the planet. The standard $g = 9{,}80665$ m/s² is already the result of that addition. Adding the centrifugal force to weight separately means counting it twice.

math.title: The math you'll need here
math.lead: Three topics: how the same two emerges by a completely different route, what exactly the cross product can and cannot do, and why the deflection grows as the square of time.

items.what: Polar coordinates: a third derivation of the same two
items.why: Our formula can be obtained without ever mentioning reference frames. Write the position of a point in the plane via the distance $r$ and angle $\theta$, differentiate twice, and carefully collect terms. In the radial part, $-r\dot\theta^{2}$ appears — this is the centrifugal term, the same $\omega^{2}r$ with the sign 'toward the center'. In the angular part, $2\dot r\dot\theta$ appears — this is Coriolis. And the two in it arises for a purely formal reason: the angular velocity enters as the product $r\dot\theta$, and the derivative of a product gives two terms, $\dot r\dot\theta$ and $r\ddot\theta$; after reducing to the angular unit vector, the first appears twice. It is useful to see the same factor obtained in three different ways — by geometry of displacement, by analyzing two mechanisms, and by the product rule. The coincidence of three independent paths is the most reliable check there is.
items.latex: \vec r = r\,\hat r \;\Longrightarrow\; \vec a = \bigl(\ddot r - r\dot\theta^{2}\bigr)\hat r + \bigl(r\ddot\theta + 2\dot r\dot\theta\bigr)\hat\theta

items.what: Cross product: why the force does no work
items.why: All behavior of the Coriolis term is read directly from the properties of the symbol $\times$. First: the result is perpendicular to both factors, so $\vec F_{\text{cor}}\perp\vec v$, so the power $\vec F\cdot\vec v$ is strictly zero — the force neither adds nor removes energy, only bends the trajectory. Second: the magnitude equals $2m\,\omega v\sin\alpha$, where $\alpha$ is the angle between the velocity and the axis; motion along the axis gives zero, motion across gives the maximum. Just don't confuse this sine with the latitude one: $\alpha$ is the angle between velocity and axis, $\varphi$ is latitude, and they coincide only for motion along a meridian. The factor $\sin\varphi$ in the Coriolis parameter is taken differently — by projecting $\vec\Omega$ itself onto the local vertical, and that is a separate step of the derivation. For a train going east, the total Coriolis force is $2m\Omega v$ entirely; only the horizontal fraction $\sin\varphi$ remains, and the vertical part is taken up by weight. Third: expanding the double product turns the mysterious $\vec\omega\times(\vec\omega\times\vec r)$ into the understandable 'minus omega squared times distance to the axis' — and also explains why the formula uses exactly $r_{\perp}$, not the full radius vector. At the pole, the distance to the axis is zero, and there is no centrifugal force at all.
items.latex: \vec\omega\times(\vec\omega\times\vec r) = \vec\omega\,(\vec\omega\cdot\vec r) - \vec r\,\omega^{2} = -\,\omega^{2}\,\vec r_{\perp}, \qquad |\vec\omega\times\vec v| = \omega v\sin\alpha

items.what: Expansion in a small parameter: where the square of time comes from
items.why: In the lemma, we replaced $\sin(\omega\,dt)$ with $\omega\,dt$ and $\cos(\omega\,dt)$ with unity; the discarded part is of order $dt^{2}$ and vanishes in the limit — this is a standard procedure. More interesting is another place. When calculating the deflection of a projectile, we take $d = \tfrac12 a t^{2}$, as if the Coriolis acceleration were constant. In reality, it rotates with the velocity, and the exact trajectory in the horizontal plane is not a parabola but an arc of a circle of radius $v/f$, called the inertial circle. Expand its deviation from a straight line in a series in the small angle $ft$ — and the first term turns out to be exactly our formula. For a projectile with a flight time of 55 s at latitude 50°, the angle $ft$ is $6.1\cdot10^{-3}$, and the relative correction $(ft)^{2}/12$ is three parts per million. The approximation here is not just good, but excessively good.
items.latex: x = R\bigl(1-\cos ft\bigr), \; R = \frac{v}{f} \;\Longrightarrow\; x = \tfrac12 f v t^{2}\Bigl[1 - \tfrac{(ft)^{2}}{12} + \dots\Bigr]

example.title: Example with numbers
example.lead: Let's calculate what artillerymen enter into firing tables as a separate line: how much the Earth manages to rotate under a flying projectile.
example.given: Latitude $\varphi = 50^\circ$ north. Range $R = 20$ km, flight time $t = 55$ s. Earth's angular velocity $\Omega = 7{,}2921\cdot10^{-5}$ rad/s. Find the lateral deflection. Then the same for the 'Paris Gun' of 1918: range 120 km, flight time 176 s, latitude of the position 49.6°.
example.law: The horizontal acceleration is $a = f\,v$, where $f = 2\Omega\sin\varphi$; the deflection during flight time is $d = \tfrac12 a t^{2} = \tfrac12 f R t$, to the right of the firing direction.

solution.text: The Coriolis parameter at this latitude. Let's also look at its reciprocal: $2\pi/f$ is the period of the inertial circle, 15.6 hours. For anything that happens faster, Coriolis only manages to give a slight nudge.
The average horizontal velocity and the acceleration itself. The number turns out to be funny — 240 times smaller than $g$; you wouldn't notice that by eye in any single second of flight.
But time works quadratically, and 55 seconds turn a funny acceleration into a quite serious distance.

The 'Paris Gun'. The range increased by a factor of 6, but the flight time only by 3.2, because the shell traveled most of the way in the rarefied stratosphere at enormous speed. The deflection goes as the product of range and time, so it increased by about 19 times.

example.answer: Sixty-one meters to the right at a range of 20 km, and almost 1.2 kilometers at a range of 120 km. In angular measure, this is the same order of magnitude: 61 m at 20 km is 3.1 milliradians, about ten arcminutes.
example.check: Is it reasonable? Let's compare with the accuracy of the gun itself: the dispersion of shells at 20 km is tens of meters across the front, so the Coriolis deflection is roughly equal to the width of the dispersion ellipse. This means the correction must be taken into account — but it does not dominate; it stands alongside corrections for wind, propellant temperature, and barrel wear. There is a well-known story about the Battle of the Falkland Islands in 1914: British ships supposedly shot wide because their tables were compiled for the Northern Hemisphere, while the battle took place in the Southern Hemisphere, where the deflection is to the left — and the error doubled. The story is nice but poorly documented: there is no confirmation in reports, and the misses at that distance are more convincingly explained by smoke, ship motion, and rangefinder performance. A cautious formulation is this: the sign change when crossing the equator is a fact, but the specific anecdote is more folklore. And one more honest caveat about the calculation itself: we only considered the horizontal velocity. The projectile also has vertical velocity, which together with the horizontal component of $\Omega\cos\varphi$ gives an additional eastward term depending on the azimuth of fire; on a symmetric trajectory it mostly cancels out, but in real tables it is computed numerically, not by a one-line formula.

constants.title: Constants of this section
constants.lead: Four numbers. The first sets everything else, the second explains why it is exactly that, the third is a meteorologist's working tool, and the fourth shows how small the centrifugal term is under our feet.

items.name: Angular velocity of Earth's rotation
items.why: It is calculated from sidereal days, not solar days: $2\pi/86\,164$, not $2\pi/86\,400$. The value slowly decreases — tidal friction on the bottom of shallow seas slows the planet by about 2 ms per century; this is also related to leap seconds, which are occasionally inserted into timekeeping: they adjust the uniform atomic scale to the unevenly rotating planet. Tides are not the only cause of irregularity: the redistribution of masses inside the Earth also perturbs rotation, which in recent years has even caused the planet to speed up slightly. For all calculations in this section, Ω can be safely considered constant.
items.mnemo: It is easier to remember in degrees: the Earth turns 15° per hour, exactly one time zone. From this, the '7.3 times ten to the minus fifth' is obtained by dividing 15° by 3600 s. Only 15° per hour is a solar day; in sidereal terms it is 15.04° per hour, and the mnemonic underestimates $\Omega$ by three-tenths of a percent.

items.name: Sidereal day
items.why: A full revolution relative to the stars, not relative to the Sun. The difference of 236 seconds accumulates because during a year the Earth manages to orbit the Sun and thereby makes one more revolution relative to the stars than relative to the Sun: 366.25 versus 365.25. It is the sidereal day that enters the period of the Foucault pendulum — at the pole it equals exactly that, not the solar day.
items.mnemo: Shorter than the ordinary day by almost four minutes. Hence the stars rise each evening four minutes earlier, and the constellations complete a full circle over the year.

items.name: Coriolis parameter at latitude 45°
items.why: The working number of all dynamic meteorology and oceanography: the horizontal acceleration equals $f v$, the radius of the inertial circle is $v/f$, and the geostrophic wind is $(1/\rho f)\,dp/dx$. At mid-latitudes it is almost always taken as a round $10^{-4}$ — the error is about three percent. The reciprocal $2\pi/f$ is the period of the inertial circle, 16.9 hours at 45°.
items.mnemo: Round $10^{-4}$ at 'our' latitudes. And a useful pair: the inertial period is 11.97 h / sin φ, and the period of the Foucault pendulum is exactly twice that, 23.93 h / sin φ.

items.name: Centrifugal acceleration at the equator
items.why: Only 0.35 percent of $g$ — that is, the planet's rotation hardly prevents us from standing. But this tiny addition over billions of years made the Earth not a sphere: the equatorial radius is 21 kilometers greater than the polar one. And it also deflects the plumb line from the direction to the planet's center: the maximum occurs at latitude 45° and is about 5.9 arcminutes.
items.mnemo: One third of a percent of g — and that was enough to shave off the poles and add twenty-one kilometers to the equator.

synthesis.title: How this relates to the rest of the course
synthesis.lead: The formula is short, but it stands at a crossroads: backward it looks to the topic of rotation, sideways to gravity and fluids, forward to instruments that measure rotation without a single moving part.

items.text: The topic 'Oscillations and rotation' introduced the very idea of inertial force: it has no source and no partner in the third law, but in its own frame it acts quite real. There we also derived $a = v^{2}/R$. Now it is clear that this is a special case of the first step of our derivation: set $dv/dt = 0$ and $\rho = R$ — only the normal part remains. And the centrifugal term $\omega^{2}r_{\perp}$ is the same thing written on the other side of the equals sign.

The most popular explanation of the second tide — 'on the far side from the Moon, a centrifugal force acts' — is tempting precisely because we have just derived this term. It gives the correct answer for the wrong reason, and the section 'Tides' in the topic 'Gravity' examines this substitution in detail. In short: the tide is created by the DIFFERENCE in attraction across the Earth's volume, and it exists regardless of the frame of reference you use. You can use the derived formula everywhere except here.

The small Rossby number of large-scale motions means that the pressure gradient is balanced not by inertia but by Coriolis: air moves almost along isobars, not across them. An estimate on a typical map: a pressure difference of one hectopascal per hundred kilometers gives $v = (1/\rho f)\,dp/dx = 10^{-3}/(1{,}2\cdot1{,}03\cdot10^{-4}) \approx 8$ m/s — exactly the wind speed that is written on the forecast. Hence also the trade winds: air flowing from the thirties toward the equator is deflected to the right and arrives at the equator not from the north but from the northeast. We do not write the equations of fluid motion here — that is the topic 'Fluids'.

The gyroscope from the second section of the topic keeps the direction of its axis and therefore senses the rotation of the base. But there is a way without a single moving part: send two light beams around a ring in opposite directions, and in a rotating frame their travel times will differ — this is the Sagnac effect, on which laser and fiber-optic gyroscopes of aircraft operate. There is no mechanics at all, and what is measured is the same $\vec\Omega$ that appears in all the formulas of this section.

curiosities.title: Fun: Try it with your hands
curiosities.lead: Two kitchen experiments, both three minutes long. The first shows the Coriolis effect in its pure form and on a large scale; the second shows that it's absent in a sink.

items.text: Place a sheet of paper on a flat plate or a pot lid—anything that spins easily on the table. Take a ruler and press it against the TABLE, not the plate, so that it runs from the center of the sheet to the edge. Spin the plate by hand at about one revolution per three seconds and, without stopping it, draw a marker along the ruler from the center outward—calmly, over half a second. Stop the plate and look at the trace. Guess in advance: how far will it deviate from the ruler?
items.answer: On the sheet, there is a noticeable arc, curving sideways by about eight to ten centimeters—that is, almost the entire length of the stroke. Let's calculate. One revolution in three seconds is $\omega \approx 2$ rad/s. The marker traveled 10 cm in half a second, so $v = 0.2$ m/s. The Coriolis acceleration is $a = 2\omega v = 0.8$ m/s², and over half a second it gives $\tfrac12 a t^{2} = 0.5\cdot0.8\cdot0.25 = 0.1$ m, that is, ten centimeters. The same answer comes without any forces: the end of the stroke ended up at a radius of 10 cm, and the sheet rotated by an angle $\omega t = 1$ radian in half a second, so the point on the sheet moved by $r\cdot\omega t = 10$ cm. But this is not an independent check; it's the same expression written twice: $\tfrac12(2\omega v)t^{2} = \omega\,(vt)\,t = r\cdot\omega t$. And both forms are only the first term in an expansion in the rotation angle, and our angle is $\omega t = 1$ radian, which is not small. The exact answer comes from the rotation itself: the end of the stroke is offset from the straight ruler by $r\sin\omega t = 10\cdot0.84 = 8.4$ cm. So the formula $\tfrac12 a t^{2}$ overestimates here by about a fifth—and it's more honest to remember that, rather than a round ten. The key point of the experiment is this: the marker moved strictly along the straight ruler, no one pushed it sideways, and yet the trace on the paper is curved. The Coriolis force is the price paid by an observer who decides to treat the rotating sheet as stationary. Now try the opposite—hold the ruler on the plate and draw the marker along it: the trace on the paper will be straight, but if you filmed it from above, in the frame it would appear curved.

items.text: Plug the sink, fill it with water, and leave it alone for about twenty minutes, without touching anything. Carefully, without splashing, pull the plug and watch which way the vortex spins. Write it down. Now fill it again, give the water a slight swirl clockwise with your hand, wait a minute for the visible motion to settle, and pull the plug again. Repeat with a counterclockwise swirl. The question is simple: what determines the direction?
items.answer: The direction of the vortex follows the swirl you imparted with your hand—even one that is no longer visible to the eye. That is the answer. Let's calculate what the Coriolis effect competes with. At latitude 45°, the vertical component of Earth's rotation is $\Omega\sin\varphi = 5.2\cdot10^{-5}$ rad/s—one revolution in 34 hours. Residual rotation of water after filling the sink from the tap easily reaches $10^{-2}$ rad/s, which is two hundred times larger, and it persists for tens of minutes because viscosity damps it slowly. The Rossby number confirms the same from another angle: $\mathrm{Ro} = v/(fL) = 0.3/(1.03\cdot10^{-4}\cdot0.2) \approx 1.5\cdot10^{4}$—the Coriolis effect is weaker than the flow's own inertia by almost fifteen thousand times. Add the asymmetric shape of the basin, the slope of the bottom, and the exact position of the drain. But honesty requires saying the opposite too: you can actually see the Coriolis effect in a drain if you try hard enough. In 1962, Ascher Shapiro in Boston took a circular tank 1.8 meters in diameter, let the water settle for a day under a lid, and opened the drain very slowly—the vortex went counterclockwise, as expected in the Northern Hemisphere. In 1965, the same setup was repeated in Sydney and the swirl was clockwise. So the effect is real, but in a kitchen it drowns in noise that is thousands of times louder.

items.h: The force that does no work but makes all the weather
items.text: We proved that the Coriolis force is perpendicular to velocity, so its power is zero: it can neither speed up nor slow down air. Then where do hurricanes come from, which in a day release more energy than all the power plants on Earth generate in the same time?
items.answer: The work is done not by the Coriolis effect but by the pressure difference—and ultimately by the Sun, which creates that difference through uneven heating. The Coriolis effect adds not a single joule to the motion; it only prevents air from reaching the center of low pressure. Without it, air would flow straight into the low-pressure area along the radius, equalizing the difference in a few hours, and that would be the end of it. With it, the inflowing stream turns and misses the center, starts circling around, the pressure difference persists, and the system lives for weeks, continuously fed by ocean heat. The rule translates into a household analogy: the steering wheel doesn't give the car a drop of fuel, but without it you won't get far. By the way, about why a hurricane gradually draws air inward instead of spinning forever: near the surface, viscous friction slightly slows the wind, the Coriolis force weakens proportionally to speed, the balance breaks, and the pressure difference pulls air inward along a spiral. It is this near-surface layer that feeds the machine with moist, warm air.

items.h: Baer's law: the right bank is steeper
items.text: Academician Karl Baer noticed in 1857 that rivers in the Northern Hemisphere flowing in a meridional direction have a right bank that is systematically steeper and more precipitous than the left—the Volga, Dnieper, Ob. He explained it by the Coriolis effect: water is pressed to the right and undercuts the right bank. How plausible is this numerically?
items.answer: Let's estimate on a train, where the numbers are more honest than in a river. A train of 500 tons travels at 200 km/h (55.6 m/s) at latitude 55°, where $f = 1.19\cdot10^{-4}$ s⁻¹. The lateral force is $F = m f v = 5\cdot10^{5}\cdot1.19\cdot10^{-4}\cdot55.6 \approx 3.3$ kN—against a weight of 4.9 meganewtons, that's seven hundredths of a percent. For one trip, it's nothing. But the force is always in one direction, and rails last for decades, and on single-track roads of tsarist construction, wear on the right rail was indeed recorded. With rivers, it's more complicated, and the honest answer is "partially." The Coriolis acceleration in a lowland river with a speed of 1 m/s is $f v \approx 1.2\cdot10^{-4}$ m/s², while the acceleration at a bend with a radius of two hundred meters at the same speed is $v^{2}/R = 5\cdot10^{-3}$ m/s², forty times larger. Therefore, meanders shape banks much more strongly. But meanders have no preferred side; they bend the channel left and right and on average give zero, while the Coriolis effect is a small but one-sided displacement, and over long stretches and geological times it accumulates. Modern hydrology considers Baer's law real but a weak effect that is easily overwhelmed by everything else at a particular bend.

items.h: Inertial circles: motion with no cause at all
items.text: Let's turn off all forces except the Coriolis effect. Then the body must move so that the acceleration is constant in magnitude and always perpendicular to velocity—and that is motion in a circle. Its radius is $v/f$, and the period $2\pi/f$ does not depend on speed or radius.
items.answer: These circles are actually seen in the ocean. A drifting buoy often does not go in a straight line but loops: at a speed of 0.2 m/s at latitude 55°, the radius is $v/f = 0.2/(1.19\cdot10^{-4}) \approx 1.7$ km, and the period is 14.6 hours, exactly what records from drifting buoys show. In the Northern Hemisphere, loops are always right-handed; in the Southern, left-handed. It's useful to understand that this motion is not caused by anything: not by wind, not by current, not by slope. It is pure inertia seen from a rotating frame—in a stationary frame, the buoy simply goes straight, and the loops are drawn by the Earth rotating beneath it. And here is where the formula breaks down. First, at the equator $f$ becomes zero, the radius becomes infinite, and the whole construction loses meaning: a separate discussion is needed there. Second, if $\mathrm{Ro}$ is of order one, neither term is dominant, and you have to solve the full equation—this is the scale of tornadoes and sea breezes, kilometers. Third, a real buoy feels friction, and its loops are not closed but spiral outward.

blocks.h: The constant ω and the lost term
blocks.text: The entire derivation is made under the assumption that the rotation is uniform. If this is not the case, the lemma gives an additional term, and a fourth force appears on the right-hand side of the second law—the Euler force. It is directed tangentially and depends not on the body's velocity or its position along the radius, but on how quickly the rotation itself changes. It is easiest to notice on a carousel that has just been turned on: the passenger is pulled backward along the direction of motion, even though they are sitting still. For the Earth, the Euler term is negligible—the day lengthens by about 2 milliseconds per century, meaning $d\Omega/dt \sim 10^{-22}$ s⁻². But in the machines for which Coriolis wrote his paper, it is quite noticeable: any acceleration or deceleration of a rotating part contributes.
blocks.latex: m\,\vec a_{\text{rel}} = \vec F + m\,\omega^{2}\vec r_{\perp} + 2m\,[\vec v_{\text{rel}}\times\vec\omega] - m\,\frac{d\vec\omega}{dt}\times\vec r

blocks.h: The plumb line deviates twice as much as our formula suggests
blocks.text: The centrifugal force deflects the plumb line from the direction to the planet's center: its horizontal component equals $\Omega^{2}R\sin\varphi\cos\varphi$, and at latitude 45° it gives an angle of $1.73\cdot10^{-3}$ radians, i.e., 5.9 arcminutes. The number is calculated honestly, but the real plumb line at this latitude is deflected from the geocentric radius by about 11.5 arcminutes—twice as much. The discrepancy is not a calculation error but a consequence of what we did not take into account: the Earth is not a sphere. The equatorial bulge of 21 kilometers attracts by itself, and its contribution to the deflection turns out to be comparable to the direct centrifugal one. A funny loop: the bulge is created by the same centrifugal force, but it acts through gravity, not kinematics. Hence a practical conclusion for geodesy—the latitude measured by the plumb line (geodetic) and the latitude measured from the planet's center (geocentric) must not be confused: at mid-latitudes they diverge by almost twelve arcminutes.

blocks.h: The Foucault pendulum turns twice as slowly as the inertial circle
blocks.text: In our derivation, a body acted on only by Coriolis force winds circles with frequency $f = 2\Omega\sin\varphi$. The plane of a Foucault pendulum, however, turns twice as slowly, at a rate of $\Omega\sin\varphi$. There is no contradiction, and it is worth understanding. The pendulum's swing is the sum of two circular motions, left and right, with equal amplitudes. Coriolis accelerates one of them by $f/2$ and slows the other by exactly the same amount. The sum of two circles with slightly different frequencies is still a segment, only slowly rotating, and its rotation speed equals half the frequency difference, i.e., $f/2 = \Omega\sin\varphi$. There is also a practical subtlety, which is why Foucault did not push the bob by hand but burned the holding thread: the slightest lateral component at launch turns the segment into a narrow ellipse, and an ellipse precesses on its own due to the nonlinearity of the suspension, and this parasitic precession can be of the same order as the useful one. That is why in museums pendulums are launched strictly from rest.

blocks.h: The body is a point, the medium is ideal
blocks.text: Two simplifications at the boundary with neighboring sections. First: we considered the body as a point, so neither moment of inertia, nor angular momentum, nor gyroscopic effects entered here—they are covered in the first two sections of the topic, and for an extended rotating body in a rotating frame the picture is much richer. Second: we have no viscosity. In a real atmosphere, near the ground friction slows the wind, the Coriolis force weakens along with the speed, and the balance with the pressure gradient is disturbed—air flows into a cyclone at an angle to the isobars, and the wind direction gradually turns with height, forming the so-called Ekman spiral. It is this surface layer, about a kilometer thick, that provides the inflow of air into the center of a hurricane. We do not write out the equations of motion for a viscous fluid here—that is a separate topic.

memo.essence: An observer in a rotating system sees the same motions but must add two forces without a source to the equation. One depends on position: $m\omega^{2}r_{\perp}$, outward from the axis. The other depends on velocity: $2m[\vec v\times\vec\omega]$, always transverse to the motion, and therefore doing no work and only able to turn. Both are obtained from the geometry of displacement over $dt$, both are the price for the right to consider the rotating floor stationary.

keyIdeas.title: Lemma on the rotating basis
keyIdeas.text: $(d\vec A/dt)_{\text{fixed}} = (d\vec A/dt)_{\text{rot}} + \vec\omega\times\vec A$ — applied twice, to $\vec r$ and to $\vec v$, and gives everything

keyIdeas.title: The two is not accidental
keyIdeas.text: The rotation of the velocity vector and the increment of the transport velocity each give $\omega v\,dt$ — two different mechanisms, the same contribution

keyIdeas.title: Only turns
keyIdeas.text: $\vec F_{\text{cor}}\perp\vec v$ always, so the power is zero: this force neither adds nor removes energy

keyIdeas.title: Measure of importance — Rossby number
keyIdeas.text: $\mathrm{Ro} = v/(fL)$: for a cyclone 0.097 and Coriolis rules, for a sink $1.5\cdot10^{4}$ and it is not visible

where: Weather: wind goes along isobars, not across; a cyclone in the northern hemisphere is spun counterclockwise, in the southern — clockwise
Trade winds: air flowing from the thirties latitudes to the equator arrives there from the northeast, not from the north
Artillery: drift of 61 m per 20 km is included in firing tables along with corrections for wind and charge temperature
Foucault pendulum: full rotation of the swing plane in 23.93 h / sin φ — 31.8 h in Paris, 48.8 h in El Kuwait
Ocean: drifting buoys wind inertial loops with radius of about a kilometer and period 11.97 h / sin φ
memo.watchOut: Three traps. First — confusing the distance to the AXIS with the distance to the center: in the centrifugal term stands $r_{\perp}$, and at the pole it is zero, although the Earth's radius there has not gone anywhere. Second — adding the centrifugal force to weight: standard $g$ already contains it, because the scales rotate with the planet, and adding it again is double counting. Third — explaining tides and the sink vortex by the centrifugal force: in the first case it is the right answer for the wrong reason, in the second — the effect is thousands of times weaker than what actually sets the direction.

quiz.q: A projectile is fired due south from a point at latitude 50° north. In which direction will it be deflected by the Coriolis force?
options: To the west: in the northern hemisphere the deflection is always to the right of the direction of motion, and to the right of south is west
To the east: the Earth rotates eastward and carries the projectile along
Nowhere: when moving along a meridian the deflection vanishes
To the south, i.e. the projectile simply overshoots: the force is directed along the velocity
quiz.why: The horizontal Coriolis force is equal to $m f v$ and stands perpendicular to the velocity, deflecting to the right in the northern hemisphere — for any direction of firing. We look south, turn right — we get west. The answer 'to the east' confuses two different things: the entrainment by rotation is already included in the transport velocity and in an inertial frame gives a straight-line flight, while the deflection is precisely what remains on top of it. The answer 'nowhere' is directly checked by the formula: it is not meridional motion that vanishes but motion along the axis of rotation, and at latitude 50° the horizontal velocity does not coincide with the axis. The answer 'the force is directed along the velocity' contradicts the fundamental property: $\vec F_{\text{cor}}\perp\vec v$, and therefore along the velocity this force gives nothing at all.
quiz.hint: The force is perpendicular to the velocity and in the northern hemisphere deflects to the right. Stand facing south and point to the right with your hand — where did you point?

quiz.q: The Coriolis force is perpendicular to the velocity for any motion. Which consequence of this is correct?
options: It does no work: it cannot change the kinetic energy of a body in a rotating frame
It does not affect the trajectory, only the readings of instruments
It is zero for a body at rest in a rotating frame, and therefore does not participate in any problems
It is always smaller than the centrifugal force, because perpendicular forces are weaker than longitudinal ones
quiz.why: The power of a force is the scalar product $\vec F\cdot\vec v$, and for perpendicular vectors it is zero. So the Coriolis force only changes the direction of the velocity and can neither accelerate nor decelerate the body. The answer about only instrument readings is grossly wrong: the trajectory is precisely what bends, the arc on a rotating sheet is direct proof. The answer about a body at rest is half true and therefore dangerous: yes, for a body at rest the force is zero (the formula contains $\vec v_{\text{rel}}$), but it is precisely moving bodies that constitute the whole subject — wind, projectile, buoy. The answer 'perpendicular forces are weaker than longitudinal ones' is simply fiction: the ratio of the Coriolis term to the centrifugal acceleration of the flow itself, $v^{2}/L$, is the Rossby number, and in a cyclone the Coriolis term is an order of magnitude larger.
quiz.hint: The power of a force is $\vec F\cdot\vec v$. What is the scalar product of two perpendicular vectors?

quiz.q: In your own words: where does the factor 2 in the formula F = 2m[v×ω] come from? Name two mechanisms, each of which gives ω·v·dt.
quiz.why: The first mechanism: the vector of relative velocity rotates together with the floor. During time $dt$ the whole system has turned by an angle $\omega\,dt$, the velocity arrow has turned with it, and the increment across the motion is $\omega v\,dt$. The second mechanism: the body has moved radially, and the velocity of the floor itself increases with radius as $\omega r_{\perp}$. Having moved outward by $v\,dt$, the body must catch up with the floor, accelerating along the circle by another $\omega v\,dt$ — otherwise it will lag behind. Two different calculations give the same answer, hence the factor is exactly 2. The same two can also be obtained by a third way, from the derivative of the product $r\dot\theta$ in polar coordinates — and the coincidence of three independent derivations is the best check of the result.
quiz.hint: One is related to the fact that the velocity vector itself rotates. The second is that the speed of the floor depends on the distance from the axis, and the body changes this distance.

quiz.q: A Foucault pendulum is suspended at latitude 60°. In how many hours will the plane of its swing make a full rotation? Take the sidereal day to be 23.93 hours. Answer in hours.
quiz.why: The plane of swing rotates at a rate $\Omega\sin\varphi$, so the period is $T = 23.93/\sin\varphi$. The sine of sixty degrees is $\sqrt{3}/2 = 0.866$, so $T = 23.93/0.866 = 27.6$ hours, i.e. about 13 degrees per hour. Check with limiting cases: at the pole the sine is one and the period is exactly the sidereal day — the pendulum swings in a fixed plane while the Earth rotates beneath it; at the equator the sine is zero, the period is infinite, there is no rotation at all. Sixty degrees is the latitude of Saint Petersburg, and the pendulum in Saint Isaac's Cathedral, which operated from 1931 to 1986, indeed rotated by about 13 degrees per hour.
quiz.hint: The period is equal to the sidereal day divided by the sine of the latitude. The sine of sixty degrees is 0.87, so the answer should be a little more than a day.

es.title: Sistema en rotación: fuerza centrífuga y Coriolis
es.subtitle: Párrafo 3 · De dónde salen las fuerzas que no tienen fuente
intro: Coloca un plato sobre la mesa, pon una hoja de papel sobre él y hazlo girar. Ahora toma una regla, presiónala contra la mesa — no contra el plato, contra la mesa — y con un rotulador traza una línea recta a lo largo de la regla a través de la hoja que gira. Retira la hoja: hay un arco en ella. La regla era recta, la mano fue recta, la mesa no se movió, y la traza es curva. Nadie empujó la hoja hacia un lado, y sin embargo registró un giro.

Este es todo el párrafo en un experimento. Un observador fijo a la hoja que gira ve un movimiento a lo largo de un arco y debe nombrar la causa: si la trayectoria se curva, entonces hay una fuerza. No podrá encontrar su fuente — no hay cuerda, ni imán, ni cuerpo vecino que ejerza esa fuerza. Qué es la fuerza de inercia y por qué no es peor que la ordinaria ya lo analizamos en el tema «Oscilaciones y rotación»; aquí no lo repetiremos, sino que calcularemos de inmediato — obtendremos todos los términos que aparecen en un sistema en rotación, y ninguno de más.

El cuerpo en este párrafo es un punto. Ni el momento de inercia ni el momento angular, que tratamos en los dos primeros párrafos del tema, nos harán falta: no se tratará de la rotación del cuerpo, sino de la rotación de la mirada sobre el cuerpo. En el camino tendremos que introducir una cosa que hasta ahora no ha aparecido en el curso: la descomposición tangencial-normal de la aceleración. Empecemos por ahí.
es.standNote: El stand del tema tiene tres modos; necesitas el tercero, «Deriva». La plataforma de radio 0,5 m gira, se lanza una bolita desde el centro, y el stand dibuja su vuelo con dos trazas a la vez: una recta en el sistema fijo y un arco en el sistema unido a la plataforma. Ambas trazas describen el mismo movimiento, la diferencia está solo en quién mira. Pon la velocidad angular a 2,0 rad/s y la velocidad de la bolita a 2,0 m/s — son los valores que analizaremos en el texto. El stand etiquetará la aceleración de Coriolis $a = 2\omega v = 8$ m/s², y la bolita, tras recorrer todo el radio en un cuarto de segundo, se desviará lateralmente 0,25 m — la mitad del radio de la plataforma. Presta atención a dos cosas. Primera: la traza recta permanece recta, hagas lo que hagas con el deslizador $\omega$, — en el sistema fijo no hay fuerza alguna y nunca la hubo. Segunda: pon $\omega = 0$, y el arco se enderezará, y el número de Rossby en el panel volará al infinito. Este es el mismo experimento de cocina del «Entretenido», solo que allí en lugar de plataforma hay un plato, y en lugar de bolita, un rotulador.

formula.name: Aceleración en un sistema rotatorio: término centrífugo y fuerza de Coriolis
formula.latex: \vec a_{\text{fijo}} = \vec a_{\text{rel}} + 2\,\vec\omega\times\vec v_{\text{rel}} + \vec\omega\times(\vec\omega\times\vec r) \qquad \vec F_{\text{cor}} = 2m\,[\vec v_{\text{rel}}\times\vec\omega]
formula.alsoKnown: Teorema de Coriolis sobre la composición de aceleraciones; aceleración centrífuga compuesta (así la llamaba el propio Coriolis). En meteorología, el mismo término se escribe mediante el parámetro de Coriolis f = 2Ω·sin φ

authors.what: en su obra «Sobre la fuerza centrífuga» fue el primero en calcular con qué fuerza un cuerpo en rotación tira de la cuerda, y obtuvo la dependencia del cuadrado de la velocidad e inversa del radio — este es el futuro tercer término de nuestra fórmula
en las ecuaciones de las mareas ya escribió un término proporcional a la velocidad de la corriente y al seno de la latitud, pero no lo destacó como un fenómeno general separado

en su artículo «Sobre las ecuaciones del movimiento relativo de los sistemas de cuerpos» obtuvo el término que faltaba en forma general y lo llamó aceleración centrífuga compuesta; no pensaba en el planeta, sino en las máquinas: ruedas hidráulicas y engranajes, donde las piezas se mueven dentro de partes rotatorias
colgó un péndulo y mostró la rotación del plano de oscilación — la primera prueba directa, de salón, de la rotación de la Tierra, que no requiere ninguna observación astronómica
trasladó todo esto a la atmósfera y explicó por qué el viento no sopla a través de las isobaras, sino a lo largo de ellas, y por qué los ciclones en los dos hemisferios giran en direcciones opuestas

formula.story: El nombre en la fórmula es de ingeniero. Coriolis enseñaba mecánica en la Escuela Politécnica y se ocupaba de la teoría de máquinas — su verdadera fama es otra: fue él quien introdujo en la física la palabra «trabajo» en el sentido actual, como fuerza multiplicada por la distancia. El problema del que surgió el término extra era de taller: cómo calcular el movimiento de una pieza que se desliza a lo largo de un radio de una rueda en rotación. Ni el tiempo, ni los océanos, ni la Tierra aparecen en el artículo de 1835. La meteorología fue conectada con este término por Ferrel veinte años después, y la propia expresión «fuerza de Coriolis» entró en uso solo alrededor de la década de 1920, en la escuela escandinava de predicción del tiempo. Es curioso también que los primeros en obtener la respuesta práctica no fueron los físicos, sino los marineros: el holandés Buys-Ballot en 1857 formuló una regla que sigue funcionando sin fórmulas: si te pones de espaldas al viento en el hemisferio norte, la zona de baja presión quedará a tu izquierda.
